cards.front: Recall a key point about Newspapers & Journalism
cards.back: Newspapers are a key media form for informing, influencing, and reflecting public opinion. They combine written, visual, and layout codes to communicate news and comment.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Newspapers & Journalism
cards.back: Tabloid vs broadsheet: tabloids (The Sun, Daily Mirror) use sensational stories, large headlines, and simple language for a mass audience. Broadsheets (The Times, Guardian) use in-depth reporting, complex language, and serious analysis for an educated audience.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Newspapers & Journalism
cards.back: News values (Galtung and Ruge): the criteria editors use to select stories — immediacy, proximity, conflict, drama, celebrity, negativity, surprise, and size/threshold.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Newspapers & Journalism
cards.back: Newspaper conventions: headline, byline, lead paragraph (who, what, where, when, why), body text, photographs with captions, and page layout (above the fold).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Newspapers & Journalism
cards.back: Headlines use linguistic devices: puns, alliteration, emotive language, and active verbs to grab attention and communicate the angle. Tabloid headlines are larger and more sensational.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Newspapers & Journalism
cards.back: News construction: all news is selected and constructed — no newspaper reports everything. The choice of stories, angle, language, and images all reflect the publication's values and target audience.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Newspapers & Journalism
cards.back: Regulation: IPSO (Independent Press Standards Organisation) regulates most UK newspapers. IMPRESS is an alternative regulator. The Leveson Inquiry (2012) examined press ethics after phone hacking scandals.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Newspapers & Journalism
cards.back: Political bias: newspapers often have political leanings — The Sun and Daily Mail traditionally support the Conservatives; The Mirror supports Labour. This affects story selection and angle.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Newspapers & Journalism
cards.back: The decline of print: circulation has fallen dramatically as audiences shift to digital. Revenue from advertising and sales has declined, leading to job losses and consolidation.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Newspapers & Journalism
cards.back: Digital transformation: newspapers now publish online, use social media, and offer subscriptions. The shift to digital has changed news consumption — 24/7 updates, multimedia content, and reader interaction.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Newspapers & Journalism
cards.back: Citizen journalism: ordinary people report news through social media, challenging traditional journalism. This democratises news but raises questions about accuracy and verification.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Newspapers & Journalism
cards.back: Fake news: deliberate misinformation spread as news, often via social media. Newspapers and fact-checking organisations work to counter this, but it remains a significant challenge.

cards.front: What should you know about media studies exam tips — newspapers & journalism?
cards.back: 1. For Newspapers & Journalism, use media terminology precisely (e.g. connotation, denotation, representation, ideology) 2. Always analyse how media language creates meaning for specific audiences 3. Reference specific examples from set products to support your analysis 4.
